solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Begins with exclusive groups at university

parts.note: sets are exclusive social groups or cliques
to be up is to be in residence at university, especially Oxford or Cambridge

explanation.surface: Someone launches a venture alongside elite university cliques.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up' meaning at university is a British idiom: you go up to Oxford and come down when you leave.
explanation.definitionFit: To set up a business or event is to establish it, so the phrasal verb works as a synonym for begins.

clue.text: Insists upon finding old deeds

parts.note: ex- is a prefix meaning former, so old
acts are deeds, things done

explanation.surface: A lawyer demands to see some ancient property deeds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deeds' looks like legal title documents; here it simply means actions.
explanation.definitionFit: To exact something is to demand it firmly, as when one exacts payment or obedience.

clue.text: Modest heraldic insignia featuring pistols for example

parts.note: modest in size means small
arms are the heraldic devices on a coat of arms

explanation.surface: A humble coat of arms happens to show pistols.
explanation.definitionFit: Small arms are firearms carried by one person, of which pistols are an example.

clue.text: Practise with Sue

definitions.meaning: to ... a trade or study is to carry it on, an older sense
to take legal action against them

explanation.surface: Practise along with a woman named Sue.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb has two senses: pursuing an activity, and taking proceedings against someone in a court of law.

clue.text: Mark with a tick by name of playwright reportedly

indicators.note: reportedly says the words are taken as heard, so the playwright's name is said aloud

parts.note: Anton Chekhov is the Russian playwright of The Seagull

explanation.surface: Someone ticks off a famous dramatist's name on a list.
explanation.definitionFit: To check off items on a list is to tick them as they are dealt with.

clue.text: Conservative aim? To embrace the start of tussle in opposition

definitions.note: a phrase standing for the verb 'be in opposition', to fight against

indicators.note: to embrace is to hug, so the first pieces wrap around what follows

parts.note: an end is an aim or goal

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter, taken here from tussle

explanation.surface: A Tory politician wonders whether his party's aim is to welcome a fight while out of power.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In opposition' sounds like a party out of office; here it stands for the act of opposing.
explanation.definitionFit: To contend is to strive against a rival, which is acting in opposition.

clue.text: Just before son quits

indicators.note: before places the first piece ahead of the second in the answer

parts.note: just and even both mean fair, equal

explanation.surface: Just before the son walks out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quits' looks like a verb about leaving; it is the adjective meaning square with each other.
explanation.definitionFit: Being quits means neither side owes the other, the same as being evens.

clue.text: Communal fund for equipment supported by both sides in theory

indicators.note: in a down answer, the first piece sits on top of and is held up by the second

parts.note: kit is gear or equipment

indicators.note: both sides of a word are its first and last letters, taken here from theory

explanation.surface: A shared pot pays for gear that everyone backs, at least on paper.
explanation.definitionFit: A kitty is a pool of money that a group contributes to and draws from.

clue.text: Cheap sarong readjusted by dandy endlessly

indicators.note: endlessly cuts off the dandy's final letter

parts.note: a fop is a dandy, a man vain about clothes

indicators.note: readjusted says the letters of sarong are put in a new order

explanation.surface: A bargain sarong is retied by a dandy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endlessly' drops the last letter of FOP to leave FO; 'readjusted' turns SARONG into RASONG.
explanation.definitionFit: Something bought for a song is bought very cheaply, an idiom from the low price of ballad sheets.

clue.text: Bill tucking into brownish-red biscuit

indicators.note: tucking into means one piece goes inside the other, as well as eating

parts.note: maroon is a dark brownish-red colour
AC, short for account, is a bill

explanation.surface: Bill eats a reddish-brown biscuit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like a man's name eating a biscuit; it is the account abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A macaroon is a small almond or coconut biscuit.

clue.text: Complete with e-books on anger

parts.note: E is taken as written and books gives NT, the New Testament
ire is anger

explanation.surface: Someone finishes reading electronic books about anger.
explanation.definitionFit: Entire means whole, with nothing missing, so complete.

clue.text: Contributing to battle ended by former PM

indicators.note: Contributing to says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A former Prime Minister brought a battle to an end.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft took 'by former PM' as the definition, but 'by' cannot replace the name in a sentence; it is a link word, and the definition is just 'former PM'.
explanation.definitionFit: Clement Attlee was the Labour Prime Minister of Britain from 1945 to 1951.

clue.text: Crack is ultimately daft for a writer like Lamb

parts.note: a crack at something is an attempt, as is an essay

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letter of daft

explanation.surface: A joke that ends up silly suits a gentle comic writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lamb' is not the animal: Charles Lamb wrote the Essays of Elia.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Lamb is best known for his essays, so he is the example of the kind of writer meant.

clue.text: Helping to make scapegoat of mimic

indicators.note: helping to make says the answer is one part of the word that follows, sitting inside it

explanation.surface: Someone imitates another to set up a fall guy.
explanation.definitionFit: To ape is to copy someone's manner, as apes were thought to imitate people.

clue.text: Crazy nun and red-hot deb dancing

indicators.note: dancing jumbles the letters, moving them around like dancers

explanation.surface: An unhinged nun and a fiery debutante take to the dance floor.
explanation.definitionFit: Round the bend is an informal idiom meaning mad.

clue.text: Henry about to stop — surprisingly unready for pursuit of suspect

parts.note: H is the symbol for the henry, the unit of inductance

indicators.note: to stop is to plug, so the letter goes into the gap in the jumbled word
surprisingly signals that the letters of unready come out rearranged

parts.note: C is short for circa, about

explanation.surface: Henry is about to halt, caught off guard during a chase.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Surprisingly' turns UNREADY into UEANDRY; 'to stop' puts C inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A hue and cry was the old public outcry raised to chase a criminal.

clue.text: Bad guy Rod played in Minder

indicators.note: played means acted out, so these letters take a new arrangement

explanation.surface: An actor named Rod plays the villain in the TV series Minder.
explanation.walkthrough: Minder was a British TV comedy-drama about a minder, a hired protector.
explanation.definitionFit: A minder is a bodyguard, someone employed to protect a person.

clue.text: Old agricultural labourer carrying home game bird

indicators.note: carrying means holding something within

parts.note: a peasant was a farm worker of the old rural order
H is a common abbreviation for home

explanation.surface: A farmhand of old takes home a bird he has shot.
explanation.definitionFit: The pheasant is a long-tailed bird shot for sport and food.

clue.text: Overcoat, fleece and shirt destroyed by duke

indicators.note: destroyed means wrecked, so the letters are broken up and rebuilt

explanation.surface: A duke ruins a coat, a fleece and a shirt.
explanation.definitionFit: A chesterfield is a man's formal overcoat, usually with a velvet collar.

clue.text: Drink providing limitless energy

indicators.note: limitless takes away both outer letters

parts.note: steam is energy, as in running out of steam

explanation.surface: A beverage that offers unlimited vigour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Limitless' strips S and M from STEAM.
explanation.definitionFit: Tea is the hot beverage brewed from leaves.

clue.text: Discovered on oddly neglected retro sink

indicators.note: in a down answer, one piece on another sits above it

parts.note: found means discovered

indicators.note: oddly neglected means skipping the odd-placed letters and keeping the even ones

explanation.surface: A retro sink is found and ignored.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oddly neglected' keeps the 2nd and 4th letters of RETRO, giving ER.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship founders when it fills with water and goes down.

clue.text: Easy victory seconds before offensive online post

indicators.note: before puts the first piece in front of the second

parts.note: a troll is a deliberately provocative internet post

explanation.surface: A walkover moments before someone posts abuse online.
explanation.definitionFit: A stroll is a game won without effort, a walkover.

clue.text: Jazz fan speaking with fellow from the French capital perhaps

indicators.note: speaking means said aloud, so the slang word is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: a cat is old slang for a jazz enthusiast
a man is a fellow
du is French for 'from the' or 'of the'

explanation.surface: A jazz enthusiast chats with a man from Paris.
explanation.walkthrough: 'From the French' is not about origin: it translates into DU.
explanation.definitionFit: Katmandu, now usually Kathmandu, is the capital of Nepal.

clue.text: Frantically busy soldier in charge

parts.note: a man is a private soldier, as in officers and men

explanation.surface: A soldier in command is frantically busy.
explanation.definitionFit: Manic describes wild, frenzied activity.

clue.text: Not available to speak about falling short in former South African province

indicators.note: falling short drops the last letter

parts.note: to talk is to speak about

explanation.surface: Someone cannot talk about failure in an old region of South Africa.
explanation.definitionFit: Natal was a province of South Africa until 1994, now KwaZulu-Natal.

clue.text: Deny getting information about speed right away

indicators.note: about means turned round, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: gen is informal British for information

indicators.note: away read as 'taken away', so the right is removed from the word for speed

parts.note: rate is speed

explanation.surface: Someone refuses to divulge details on speed at once.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' reads GEN backwards as NEG; 'away' takes R out of RATE. 'Right away' looks like 'immediately'.
explanation.definitionFit: To negate is to deny or nullify a claim.

clue.text: Unable to find a denial in pious platitudes

indicators.note: in places one piece inside another

parts.note: cant is hypocritical pious talk
no is a denial

explanation.surface: One can find no refusal in sanctimonious talk.
explanation.definitionFit: Cannot means is not able to.

clue.text: Command at the end ignored by soldiers of Mussolini, for instance

indicators.note: the final letter is left off

parts.note: to dictate is to command
OR stands for other ranks, soldiers who are not officers

explanation.surface: Mussolini's soldiers ignored an order in the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Mussolini ruled Italy as an absolute dictator.

clue.text: He makes insistent demands with criticism Lear's answer dismissed

parts.note: stick is informal for harsh criticism

indicators.note: dismissed means sent out, so a letter goes

parts.note: Lear's is read as 'Lear has', giving the king's name

explanation.surface: King Lear's response is waved away with blame.
explanation.definitionFit: A stickler insists on exact standards, demanding they be followed.

clue.text: Practises a form of singing? Yes old style

definitions.note: a verb phrase, matching the third-person verb in the answer

indicators.note: style is to shape, so the letters are fashioned into a new order

explanation.surface: A singer agrees to a traditional technique.
explanation.definitionFit: Yodelling is an Alpine singing style switching between chest voice and falsetto.
